sections.heading: The binomial series for negative and fractional powers

questions.q: Expand $(1+x)^{-1}$ up to the term in $x^3$, using $(1+x)^n\approx1+nx+\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2+\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3$.
Expand $(1+x)^{1/2}$ up to the term in $x^3$.
questions.answer: With $n=\dfrac{1}{2}$: coefficient of $x^2$ is $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{8}$; coefficient of $x^3$ is $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)}{6}=\dfrac{1}{16}$. So $(1+x)^{1/2}\approx1+\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{8}+\dfrac{x^3}{16}$.

questions.q: Expand $(1-x)^{-3}$ up to the term in $x^2$.
questions.answer: Write $(1+u)^{-3}$ with $u=-x$: coefficient of $u$ is $-3$, coefficient of $u^2$ is $\dfrac{(-3)(-4)}{2}=6$. So $1-3(-x)+6(-x)^2=1+3x+6x^2$.

questions.q: Expand $(1+x)^{-4}$ up to the term in $x^2$.
questions.answer: With $n=-4$: coefficient of $x$ is $-4$; coefficient of $x^2$ is $\dfrac{(-4)(-5)}{2}=10$. So $(1+x)^{-4}\approx1-4x+10x^2$.

sections.heading: Validity conditions for the binomial series

questions.q: State the range of values of $x$ for which the binomial expansion of $(1+x)^{-2}$ is valid.
questions.answer: The expansion of $(1+x)^n$ for non-integer or negative $n$ is valid for $|x|<1$, i.e. $-1<x<1$.

questions.q: State the range of values of $x$ for which the expansion of $(3+x)^{-1}$ converges, given that after factoring, the general form requires $\left|\dfrac{x}{3}\right|<1$.

sections.heading: Using series expansions to approximate values

questions.q: Use $(1+x)^{1/2}\approx1+\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{8}$ to approximate $\sqrt{1.02}$, to four decimal places.
Use $(1+x)^{-1}\approx1-x+x^2-x^3$ to approximate $\dfrac{1}{1.05}$, to four decimal places.
Use the geometric series $(1-x)^{-1}\approx1+x+x^2+x^3$ (the binomial series with $n=-1$) to approximate $\dfrac{1}{0.98}$, to four decimal places.
questions.answer: Writing $\dfrac{1}{0.98}=(1-x)^{-1}$ with $x=0.02$: $1+0.02+0.0004+0.000008\approx1.0204$, matching the exact value $\dfrac{1}{0.98}\approx1.020408$.

questions.q: Use $(1+x)^{-1}\approx1-x+x^2$ to approximate $\dfrac{1}{1.01}$, to four decimal places.
Expand $(4+x)^{1/2}$ up to the term in $x^2$, by writing $(4+x)^{1/2}=4^{1/2}\left(1+\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^{1/2}$.
Expand $(2-3x)^{-1}$ up to the term in $x^2$, by writing $(2-3x)^{-1}=2^{-1}\left(1-\dfrac{3x}{2}\right)^{-1}$, and state the range of validity.
Expand $(1+2x)^{-2}$ up to the term in $x^2$, and state the range of validity.
questions.answer: With $n=-2$, $u=2x$: coefficient of $u$ is $-2$, coefficient of $u^2$ is $\dfrac{(-2)(-3)}{2}=3$. So $1-2(2x)+3(2x)^2=1-4x+12x^2$. Validity: $|2x|<1$, i.e. $|x|<\dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.q: Expand $(9-x)^{1/2}$ up to the term in $x^2$, by writing $(9-x)^{1/2}=9^{1/2}\left(1-\dfrac{x}{9}\right)^{1/2}$.
Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=\cos x$ up to the term in $x^4$, using $f(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+\dfrac{f''(0)}{2!}x^2+\dfrac{f'''(0)}{3!}x^3+\dfrac{f^{(4)}(0)}{4!}x^4$.
Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=e^{2x}$ up to the term in $x^3$.
Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=\ln(1-x)$ up to the term in $x^3$.
Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=\sin(2x)$ up to the term in $x^3$, using $\sin u\approx u-\dfrac{u^3}{6}$ with $u=2x$.

sections.heading: Building new series from known ones

questions.q: Using $e^x\approx1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}$, find the Maclaurin series for $e^{-x^2}$ up to the term in $x^4$, by substituting $-x^2$ for $x$.
questions.answer: Substituting $u=-x^2$ into $1+u+\dfrac{u^2}{2}$ (the cubic term in $u$ would give $x^6$, beyond the required order): $1+(-x^2)+\dfrac{(x^4)}{2}=1-x^2+\dfrac{x^4}{2}$.

questions.q: Given $\sin x\approx x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}$ and $(1+u)^{-1}\approx1-u+u^2$, find the Maclaurin series for $\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}$ up to the term in $x^2$ (using $u=\sin x\approx x$ to this order).
questions.answer: Treating $u=\sin x\approx x$ up to $x^2$ order: $\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}\approx1-x+x^2$.

questions.q: Using $\dfrac{1}{1-x}\approx1+x+x^2+x^3$, differentiate term by term to find the Maclaurin series for $\dfrac{1}{(1-x)^2}$ up to the term in $x^2$.
questions.answer: Differentiating the left side gives $\dfrac{1}{(1-x)^2}$; differentiating the right side term by term: $1+2x+3x^2+\cdots$. So $\dfrac{1}{(1-x)^2}\approx1+2x+3x^2$.

questions.q: Using $\ln(1+x)\approx x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}$, find the Maclaurin series for $\ln(1+2x)$ up to the term in $x^3$, by substituting $2x$ for $x$.

sections.heading: Using series to approximate definite integrals

questions.q: Use $\cos x\approx1-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^4}{24}$ to approximate $\int_0^{0.5}\cos x\,dx$, to four decimal places, and compare with the exact value $\sin(0.5)\approx0.4794$.
questions.answer: Integrating term by term: $\left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{x^5}{120}\right]_0^{0.5}=0.5-\dfrac{0.125}{6}+\dfrac{0.03125}{120}\approx0.5-0.020833+0.00026\approx0.4794$, matching $\sin(0.5)$ closely.

questions.q: Given the standard result $(1-x^2)^{-1/2}\approx1+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{3x^4}{8}$, approximate $\int_0^{0.2}(1-x^2)^{-1/2}\,dx$, to four decimal places, and compare with the exact value $\arcsin(0.2)\approx0.2014$.
questions.answer: Integrating term by term: $\left[x+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{3x^5}{40}\right]_0^{0.2}=0.2+\dfrac{0.008}{6}+\dfrac{3(0.00032)}{40}\approx0.2+0.001333+0.000024\approx0.2014$, matching $\arcsin(0.2)$ closely.

sections.heading: A well-designed word problem: relativistic momentum correction

questions.q: This question has three parts. In special relativity, the momentum correction factor is $\gamma=\left(1-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\right)^{-1/2}$, where $v$ is speed and $c$ is the speed of light. (a) Using the binomial expansion with $u=-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$, show that $\gamma\approx1+\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}+\dfrac{3v^4}{8c^4}$ for small $\dfrac{v}{c}$. (b) A satellite travels at $v=7000$ m/s, with $c=3\times10^8$ m/s. Using only the first-order approximation $\gamma\approx1+\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}$, find $\gamma-1$, to three significant figures, in standard form. (c) Explain, by comparing orders of magnitude, why the second term $\dfrac{3v^4}{8c^4}$ is negligible for this satellite compared to the first-order term.
questions.answer: (a) With $n=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $u=-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$: $(1+u)^{-1/2}\approx1-\dfrac{1}{2}u+\dfrac{3}{8}u^2=1-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\right)+\dfrac{3}{8}\left(\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\right)^2=1+\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}+\dfrac{3v^4}{8c^4}$. (b) $\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}=\dfrac{(7000)^2}{(3\times10^8)^2}=\dfrac{4.9\times10^7}{9\times10^{16}}\approx5.44\times10^{-10}$. $\gamma-1\approx\dfrac{1}{2}(5.44\times10^{-10})\approx2.72\times10^{-10}$. (c) The second term equals $\dfrac{3}{8}\left(\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\right)^2\approx\dfrac{3}{8}(5.44\times10^{-10})^2\approx1.11\times10^{-19}$, roughly nine orders of magnitude smaller than the first-order term ($2.72\times10^{-10}$) — since $\dfrac{v}{c}$ is already extremely small, squaring the ratio in the second term makes it astronomically smaller still, so it can safely be ignored.
